## How to use this

The code from Lecture 17, filled in, with the numbers it produces.

. . .

Optimizers are numerical, so your last decimal place may differ from mine.
Anything beyond that is worth asking about.

::: {.notes}
Posted after class so nobody is left wondering whether their answer was right.
:::

## Setting up {.smaller}

```{r}
library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

nll_2019 <- function(p){
  -dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}

p_vec <- seq(0.55, 0.90, by = 0.001)
nll_vec <- nll_2019(p_vec)

c(occupancy_rows = nrow(occ), count_rows = nrow(counts))
```

## Finding the interval {.smaller}

```{r}
best <- min(nll_vec)

range(p_vec[nll_vec <= best + 1.92])
```

. . .

Read from the inside out: `nll_vec <= best + 1.92` is a TRUE or FALSE for every
candidate; `p_vec[...]` keeps the candidates that were TRUE; `range()` returns
the smallest and the largest.

. . .

Not symmetric around 0.732: about 0.109 below and 0.093 above. The curve is
steeper on the side nearer 1.

## The shortcut {.smaller}

```{r}
p_hat <- 52 / 71
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 71)
p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
```

Close to the curve's answer. Now the pewee, 3 of 71:

```{r}
p_hat <- 3 / 71
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 71)
p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
```

A **negative** lower limit, for a probability.

## The profile {.smaller}

```{r}
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")

occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied,
                 n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)

m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
              data = occ_data)

b_vec <- seq(-0.10, -0.03, by = 0.005)
prof_nll <- numeric(length(b_vec))

for (i in seq_along(b_vec)) {
  fit_i <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2,
                start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
                fixed = list(b = b_vec[i]),
                data = occ_data)
  prof_nll[i] <- fit_i@min
}
```

## The slice, and both together {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.8
a_hat <- coef(m_occ)["a"]
slice_nll <- numeric(length(b_vec))

for (i in seq_along(b_vec)) {
  slice_nll[i] <- occ_nll2(c(a_hat, b_vec[i]), occ$n_occupied,
                           occ$n_routes, occ$elapsed)
}

plot(b_vec, prof_nll - m_occ@min, type = "b", ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "b", ylab = "NLL above the minimum")
abline(h = 1.92, lty = 2)
points(b_vec, slice_nll - m_occ@min, type = "b", col = "red")
```

## Why the slice is narrower {.smaller}

The slice crosses 1.92 much closer to the best $b$, so its interval is less than
half as wide.

. . .

It holds $a$ at one value. But $a$ and $b$ are strongly correlated (about
−0.89): a curve that starts higher has to fall faster. The profile lets $a$
adjust at every $b$, so it finds a lower NLL there and accepts a wider range of
$b$.

. . .

The slice is not wrong about the surface. It is answering a different question,
"how plausible is this $b$ **if $a$ is known exactly**?", and nobody knows $a$
exactly.

## `confint()` {.smaller}

```{r}
confint(m_occ)
confint(m_occ, method = "quad")
```

## Back-transforming {.smaller}

```{r}
exp(confint(m_occ)["b", ])
1 - exp(confint(m_occ)["b", ])
```

The odds of occupancy fall by between about 4.3% and 7.7% a year. Zero is not in
the interval for $b$, so a flat line is ruled out.

## Development {.smaller}

```{r}
urban_nll2 <- function(params, y, u){
  mu <- params[1] * exp(params[2] * u)
  -sum(dnbinom(y, mu = mu, size = params[3], log = TRUE))
}
parnames(urban_nll2) <- c("mu0", "b", "size")

m_urban <- mle2(minuslogl = urban_nll2,
                start = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                data = list(y = counts$count, u = counts$frac_built),
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(mu0 = 0.1, b = -20, size = 0.05),
                upper = c(mu0 = 100, b = 20, size = 50))

confint(m_urban)
log(2) / abs(confint(m_urban)["b", ])
```

Counts halve with every 18% to 26% of development. The steeper end of $b$ gives
the shorter halving distance, so the two ends swap places.

## Additional practice: coverage {.smaller}

```{r}
interval_from_curve <- function(k, n, p_vec){
  nll <- -dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p_vec, log = TRUE)
  range(p_vec[nll <= min(nll) + 1.92])
}

set.seed(17)
p_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, by = 0.001)
lower <- numeric(100)
upper <- numeric(100)

for (i in 1:100) {
  k <- rbinom(1, size = 71, prob = 0.73)
  ci <- interval_from_curve(k, 71, p_grid)
  lower[i] <- ci[1]
  upper[i] <- ci[2]
}

mean(lower < 0.73 & upper > 0.73)
```

About 0.95, give or take a few, from 100 tries.

## Step 5: a rare species, with the shortcut {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(17)
lower <- numeric(1000)
upper <- numeric(1000)

for (i in 1:1000) {
  k <- rbinom(1, size = 71, prob = 0.03)
  p_hat <- k / 71
  se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 71)
  lower[i] <- p_hat - 1.96 * se
  upper[i] <- p_hat + 1.96 * se
}

mean(lower < 0.03 & upper > 0.03)    # how often it catches the truth
mean(upper <= 0.03)                  # missed by being entirely too low
mean(lower < 0)                      # proposed a negative probability
```

## What step 5 shows {.smaller}

The shortcut is meant to catch the truth 95% of the time. With a rare species it
falls well short, and its misses are lopsided: almost all of them sit entirely
below the truth.

. . .

The worst case is **zero** sightings, which happens about one survey in nine
here. Then $\hat{p} = 0$, the standard error is 0, and the "interval" is the
single point 0: complete certainty, from no data.

. . .

The interval from the likelihood curve has neither problem. It fails least in
exactly the situation where people most need it: when the species is rare.
